title: Lucena and Philidor: the two rook endings to know
outcomes: Explains in plain words how the attacker wins with a pawn on the seventh (Lucena) and how the defender draws with the rook on the sixth rank (Philidor)
Avoids two tempting errors in the Lucena position: promoting at once and blocking a check with a loose rook
Knows the Philidor check from behind needs a rook placement that White's rook cannot punish

steps.text: Two rook endings to know. In **Lucena** the pawn stands on the seventh, your king is in front of it and the enemy king is cut off; you win by getting the king out of the way of checks. In **Philidor** the defender keeps the rook on the sixth rank and checks from behind once the pawn advances. Both are plans with conditions.

steps.caption: Lucena-type: White to move wins. One winning line is shown.

line.say: A rook check pushes Black's king away.
The rook goes to the fourth rank.
White's king steps out of the queening square.
Black's rook checks along the f-file.
The king steps off the file.
Black's rook checks again, now along the e-file.

claims.statement: White wins from the start position.

steps.text: **Conditions.** Lucena needs a pawn on the seventh, your king in front and the enemy king cut off. Promoting at once, or blocking a check with a loose rook, throws the win away. **Philidor** is a plan: a rook on the sixth rank is a good default, not the only drawing idea. Its check from behind fails if White's rook can capture it.

steps.title: Same Philidor move, rook one rank apart
steps.prompt: White's pawn is on e6. Black plays Ra1. Does it hold if White's rook is on h2? On h1? Predict, then check.
In which position did you want to promote or to check at once? What did you not look at before you moved: the rook's safety, or what the other rook could take?
